newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi dinar sinks, prices soar on UN remarks.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi dinar sinks, prices soar on UN remarks.

text.p: A UN announcement of further delay to a long-awaited "oil-for-food" deal because of security fears in north Iraq pushed up prices of essential commodities in Baghdad and weakened the dinar on Friday, traders said.

Trading was sluggish in Shurja, Baghdad's commercial hub, as buyers and sellers struggled to weigh the impact of a statement by a senior UN official on Wednesday postponing the implementation of the deal until the United Nations deems that security in northern Iraq has improved.
The dinar slipped to nearly 1,700 against the U.S. dollar from about 1,550 on Wednesday and traders said it would take time to stabilise again.
A kilogram (2.2 lb) of sugar jumped to 800 dinars from 650 last week and a kg of rice went up to 750 dinars up from 600. A tray of 30 eggs was sold at 3,200 dinars from 2,900.

Street vendors lined the wide pavements of Shurja market, shouting new prices at top of their voices. Women shoppers strode by, some murmuring words of complaint, others cursing the UN and the United States accusing them of delaying the agreement.
"It is really unfair that the UN which is supposed to help us is postponing the sale of our oil," said Um Khalid, a woman shopper who walked out of the market empty-handed.

UN Under-Secretary-General Chinmaya Gharekhan said on Wednesday that conditions in northern Iraq were not yet satisfactory for the start of the plan, which allows Iraq to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine for its impoverished population.
A senior Iraqi ruling Baath party member, Saad Qassim Hammoudi on Thursday dismissed the UN statement saying it was "unacceptable and unconvincing."
The UN official in Baghdad responsible for overseeing humanitarian aid to Iraq told Reuters last week he believed relief work could proceed in the north.

Gualtiro Fulcheri, the UN humanitarian coordinator said he had been reassured that the Kurdish Democratic Party of Masoud Barzani which took control of the north last month with support from Baghdad, could ensure security for aid workers.
Other UN officials in Baghdad say relief work has continued unchanged in more than 95 percent of the northern areas.

The UN announcement also dented Iraq's latest efforts to improve its battered currency. The Central Bank on October 2 allowed state banks to sell hard currency in exchange for the dinar for the first time.
When the measures were first implemented, the dinar surged to 1,370 against the dollar up from 1,550 prior to its application. Then it started sinking again.
"Because these banks sell only a limited amount of dollars each day, they failed to improve the dinar's value," one trader said.

The dinar's value on Friday was the lowest since Iraq and the UN started talks on how to implement their "oil-for-food" formula. The volatile currency enjoyed a brief respite and at times soared to about 500 to the dollar from 3,000 early in the year.
Prior to U.N. trade sanctions, imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait, the dinar was an oil-backed currency worth 3.1 dollars.
